cas: ═══ Computer Algebra System (CAS) ═══
JC2 features a powerful, exact Computer Algebra System for symbolic mathematics.
★ The Boundary: Numerical vs. Symbolic Computation
JC2 strictly separates Numerical and Symbolic domains:
• Numerical (Default): Variables hold values (x = 5). Expressions evaluate
immediately to numbers, matrices, or fractions.
• Symbolic (CAS): Variables hold AST nodes (x = sym("x")). Expressions
build algebraic trees instead of evaluating.
You cross from Numerical → Symbolic by using `sym("x")` or string variables.
You cross from Symbolic → Numerical by using `evalf()`, `subs()`, or `toFunc()`.
★ Automatic Symbolic Promotion
• Fractional Powers: Exact integers or fractions raised to fractional powers
(e.g., 2^(1/2)) no longer degrade to floating-point `double`. If they cannot
be evaluated exactly, they automatically promote to a symbolic expression.
• Function Nodes: Only standard built-in math functions (sin, cos, exp, log,
sqrt, etc.) can be captured as symbolic nodes (`SymFunc`). Passing a symbolic
variable to a user-defined function or an incompatible built-in will either
evaluate it immediately or throw a TypeError.
Symbolic Variables & Expressions
x = sym("x")                 Create a symbolic variable
expr = x^2 + 2*x + 1         Build exact symbolic expressions
cas.subs(expr, x, 5)         Substitute x with 5 → 36 (Strings like "x" also work!)
cas.subs(x + y, [x, y], [1, 2]) Multiple substitution
★ Variable Name Inputs
All CAS functions (diff, integ, limit, solve, taylor, polyDiv, etc.) now
accept direct symbolic variables instead of just strings.
Example: cas.diff(x^2, x) is perfectly equivalent to cas.diff(x^2, "x").

cas.factor(x^4 - 1)          → (x - 1) * (x + 1) * (x^2 + 1) (Cantor-Zassenhaus)

cas.contract(2*log(x) + log(y)) → log(x^2 * y)
cas.trigsimp(sin(x)^2 + cos(x)^2) → 1

of the polynomial `poly`. Essential for exact symbolic

★ Constants & Limitations:
• PI, E, and i are now parsed as exact symbolic constants in the CAS engine
to prevent premature floating-point evaluation. Calling evalf(sym("i"))
will evaluate it to the complex number 1i.
• solve now exactly solves high-degree binomial equations (ax^n + b = 0),
returning all complex roots using Euler's formula (E and PI).
• For high-degree irreducible polynomials, solve returns exact `RootOf`
algebraic number nodes. For robust numerical root-finding, use `solveE`.

Functions are compiled into bytecode closures executed by the VM.

★ Recursion: Local functions automatically capture their own name by reference,

Destructuring Parameters
You can directly destructure dicts, lists, or arrays in the parameter list.
This automatically unpacks the passed argument into local variables.

scope: ═══ Variable Scoping & Protection Rules ═══
★ Scope Modifiers Quick Summary
Modifier | Scope Bound | Memory Lifecycle       | Capture Semantics
(none)   | Function    | Destroyed on return    | Auto-Local (Shadows outer)
local    | Block {}    | Destroyed on block end | Strict Block Isolation
ref      | Outer/Global| Tied to outer variable | Mutates outer directly
state    | Closure     | Persistent across calls| Private State Machine
Default Behaviors
• Top Level (REPL): Variables are global. Blocks ({}, for, while) do NOT
create isolated scopes by default.
• Inside Functions: New assignments are Auto-Local to the function.
They survive block boundaries but are destroyed when the function returns.
Redeclaration & Shadowing
• Redeclaration: It is a SyntaxError to explicitly redeclare a variable
(using local, state, ref, or const) if it already exists in the SAME scope.
local x = 1; local x = 2   // ✗ SyntaxError: Variable 'x' has already been declared
x = 1; state x = 2         // ✗ SyntaxError
• Reassignment: Ordinary assignments without modifiers are perfectly fine.
local x = 1; x = 2         // ✓ OK (Reassignment)
• Shadowing: You CAN declare a variable with the same name in an INNER scope.
local x = 1; if (true) { local x = 2 }  // ✓ OK (Inner x shadows outer x)
• Self-Assignment Capture: When shadowing, idioms like `local x = x` or
`state x = x` are perfectly safe. The right side evaluates BEFORE the new
variable is registered, capturing the outer value to initialize the inner one.
★ Recommendation: While legal, prefer standalone declarations like `local x`
or `state x` for direct capture, or use a new name (`local y = x + 1`) to
improve performance and semantic clarity.
Strict Block Scope (local)
Restricts a variable strictly to the current block ({}, if, for, while).
if (true) { local temp = 100 }
print(temp)  // ✗ Error: temp is undefined
• Variable Routing: Ordinary assignments (y = 2) inside blocks bypass the
block and attach to the function/global scope. Only `local` traps them.
• Standalone Capture: `local a` without assignment will automatically capture
the value of the outer variable `a` to initialize the new block-scoped `a`.
(Equivalent to the explicit `local a = a` idiom, but faster and preferred).
• Closure Safety: If a closure captures a `local` variable, its physical
memory lives on inside the closure, but its name is destroyed.
Upward Scope Resolution (ref)
Binds a variable to an OUTER scope variable across function boundaries.
counter = 0
bump() = ref counter += 1      // Modifies outer 'counter' directly
• Capture Semantics: Local variables are captured by physical memory.
Global variables are captured by name (late-binding).
• Standalone: `ref a;` binds to outer `a`. Throws immediately if undefined.
• Parameters: `addOne(ref x) = { x += 1 }` forces pass-by-reference.
When calling `addOne(val)`, the outer variable `val` is modified directly.
If a literal or expression is passed (e.g., `addOne(5)`), it safely degrades
to pass-by-value.
Closures & State Semantics (state)
Gives a closure PRIVATE PERSISTENT memory. The outer scope is untouched.
f() = { state n = 0; n += 1; return n }
• state x = expr  : Evaluates `expr` EXACTLY ONCE on the first call.
Idiom: `state x = x` safely captures the outer `x` as the
initial private state, avoiding 'uninitialized' errors.
(However, standalone `state x` is faster and preferred).
• state x += expr : Captures outer `x` once, adds `expr` ON EVERY CALL.
• Standalone      : `state a;` captures `a` EXACTLY at definition time.
Throws IMMEDIATELY at definition time if `a` is undefined.
Destructuring Modifiers
Each target variable can independently carry a scope modifier:
[ref a, state b, local c, const d, e] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
{x: ref px, y: state py, z: const pz} = point
Modifiers can also be applied to the entire destructuring pattern:
const local [a, b] = [1, 2]
state [x, y] = compute_once()
Namespaces (Dynamic Modules)
const Math = namespace {
local seed = 12345         // Private (not exported)
const PI = 3.14            // Public immutable
add(a, b) = a + b          // Public method
• Anonymous & Sugar: `namespace Math {}` is sugar for `Math = namespace {}`.
• Strict Same-Line Rule: For anonymous namespaces, the `{` MUST be on the same line as `namespace`.
• Self-Reference: Inside the block, `namespace` evaluates to the namespace itself.
• Dynamic: Add/modify/delete members at runtime (Math.E = 2.718).
• Dict-Like: Supports keys(), values(), for-in loops.
• Freezing: `freeze(Math)` locks it, making it hashable.
• Keywords: Unlike classes and enums, you CANNOT use keywords as function/variable
names directly inside a namespace block (because it is a normal execution block).
To use a keyword name, assign it externally: `Math.match = ...`.
Constants & Built-ins
• const: `const G = 9.81`. Strictly immutable. Cannot be reassigned AND
cannot be deleted using the `delete` keyword.
★ Pass-by-Reference Protection: If a const variable is passed to a function
expecting a `ref` parameter, it safely degrades to pass-by-value to protect
its immutability.
Can be combined with scope modifiers:
`const local x = 1` : Block-scoped constant.
`const ref x`       : Read-only view of an outer variable.
`const state x = 1` : Lazy, read-only persistent state (evaluates once).
Function Parameters:
`f(const x) = ...`  : Prevents accidental reassignment of `x` inside `f`.
• System Constants: PI, E, i, I can be overwritten/deleted.
Restore via `resetConst()` or factory functions like `pi()`.
• Built-ins: Can be freely shadowed by user variables. Built-ins themselves
cannot be deleted. `delete sin` only removes the shadowing variable.
★ Variable Lifecycle Summary
Entity            Overwrite?   Delete?    Recover?
User variable     ✓            ✓          —
const variable    ✗            ✗          —
System constant   ✓            ✓          resetConst() / pi()
Built-in func     shadow       ✗          delete shadowing var

L.filter(f)             Keep elements where f(x) is truthy → new list
L.reduce(f)             Left fold using first element as initial
L.reduce(f, init)       Left fold with explicit accumulator

L.all(f)                true if ALL f(x) are truthy

L.join(", ")            Join all elements into a string
zip(L1, L2)             Pair-wise merge → list of 2-element lists

When to use list vs Array?
Array   [1, 2, 3]        Homogeneous doubles. Fast math. Use for numerics.
list    list(1, "a")     Heterogeneous. Use for mixed data.

Unlike arrays/matrices (which are passed by value and deep-copied),
L2 = L1                   // L2 and L1 share the same data

modify it (push, pop, L[i]=) will throw an error.
isFrozen(L)             Returns true if the list is locked, false otherwise.
val(L)                  Creates a deep-copy snapshot of the list (and all
nested containers), freezes the new copy, and returns it.
Perfect for safely passing data to untrusted functions.
There is no "unfreeze" function. Use copying to change lock states:
Syntax        Depth         Lock State          Best For...
b = a         Zero (Ref)    Same as source      Fast passing, default high-perf state.
b = a[:]      Shallow       Outer unfrozen      1D cloning, simple unfrozen shell.
b = copy(a)   Deep          Same as source      Exact deep clone, preserving lock states.

dict: ═══ Dictionary (Key-Value Store) ═══
dicts store unordered key-value mappings in JC2. Keys can be ANY hashable type
(strings, numbers, instances with __hash__, or frozen containers). Values can
be of any type.
Creation
d = dict()                          Empty dictionary
d = {name: "Alice", age: 30}        Literal syntax (recommended)
d = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}    Quoted string keys also work
d = {x: x^2 for (x in range(5))}    Dict comprehension
Shorthand Properties (Variables directly to dict):
name = "Bob"; age = 25
d = { name, age }                 → {"name": "Bob", "age": 25}
For computed keys (using a variable's value as the key), wrap it in
parentheses or use the function form:
d = dict(dynamic_key, 42)         → {"[1]": 42}
Block vs. dict Ambiguity Resolution
Because `{ ... }` is used for both code blocks and dictionaries, JC2 uses
a smart lookahead scanner to resolve ambiguities:
1. Explicit dicts: If it contains a colon `:` at the top level, it's a dict.
{ [1, 2]: "matrix" }         → dict
2. Explicit Blocks: If it contains a semicolon `;`, assignment `=`, or
ternary `?` at the top level, it's a Block.
{ a = 1 }                    → Block
3. Pure Shorthand dicts: If it contains ONLY identifiers, scope modifiers
(local/ref/state/const), rest patterns (...), and commas, it's a dict.
{}                           → Empty dict
{a, b}                       → Shorthand dict {"a": a, "b": b}
{local a, ...rest}           → Shorthand dict
4. Complex Expressions: If it contains numbers, strings, operators, or
function calls without a colon `:`, it's parsed as a Block.
{ 1, 2 }                     → Block (comma expression)
{ a + 1 }                    → Block
* Tip: If you want a single-statement block that returns a variable,
always add a semicolon to avoid it being parsed as a shorthand dict:
{ a; }                       → Block returning 'a'
Access & Modification
d["key"]                            Read / Write the value
d["key"] += 1                       Compound assignment directly on the value
d - @{"key1", "key2"}               Key omission (returns a NEW dict without the specified keys)
d - ["key1", "key2"]                Key omission using a list
d - {key1: 1}                       Key omission using another dict (ignores values)
* Note: d[a] evaluates the variable 'a' and uses its value as the key.
If you want the literal string "a", use d["a"]. For convenience,
you can also use the dot operator: d.a (which is identical to d["a"]).
Dot Operator Syntax Sugar
The dot operator works identically to bracket syntax for string keys:
d.name                     → "Alice"     (same as d["name"])
d.age = 31                 → modifies    (same as d["age"] = 31)
d.score = 95               → adds new key
★ Keywords as Keys:
After a dot `.`, any language keyword (like `match`, `class`, `in`) is safely
treated as a normal identifier. E.g., `d.match = 1` is perfectly valid.
Inspection & Manipulation
add(d, "key", val)                  Inserts or updates a key-value pair
remove(d, "key")                    Removes the key (throws error if absent)
discard(d, "key")                   Removes the key (silent if absent)
clear(d)                            Erases all entries
len(d) / d.dictSize() / d.size()    Number of key-value entries
type(d)                             Returns "dict"
d.hasKey("key") / d.has("key")      Returns true if the key exists
d.removeKey("key")                  Removes the key (throws error if absent)
d.keys()                            Returns all keys as a list
d.values()                          Returns all values as a list
d.dictPairs()                       Returns a list of @[key, value] pairs
d1.dictMerge(d2)                    Merges d2 into d1 (mutates d1 in-place)
d1 + d2                             Returns a NEW dict merging d1 and d2 (right side overwrites left on key conflict)
d - keys                            Returns a NEW dict with specified keys removed. 'keys' can be a set, list, or dict.
Iteration & Membership
for (k in d) { ... }             Iterate over keys
"key" in d                       Returns true if the key exists, false otherwise
Destructured iteration (extracts key-value pairs simultaneously):
for ([k, v] in d) {
print(k, "=", v)
Reference Semantics & GC
Identical to lists, dicts are passed by reference.
d2 = d1
d2.a = 99                 // d1.a is now also 99
dicts are fully tracked by the VM's Garbage Collector. Therefore, creating a
graph where dict A points to dict B, and dict B points back to dict A will
never cause a memory leak when they go out of scope.
Immutability & Hashing (Native Value Hashing)
JC2 uses a high-performance Native Value Hashing architecture.
Keys are hashed directly by their semantic value, meaning `1.0`, `int(1)`,
and `frac(1,1)` will all perfectly collide and map to the exact same key!
Keys MUST be hashable. Valid keys include:
• Numbers (double, int, fraction, complex, basenum)
• Strings and Symbolic Expressions
• Frozen containers (frozen list, dict, set)
• Functions, Classes, and Namespaces (hashed by reference)
• Class instances (ONLY if frozen, or if they define a `__hash__` dunder method)
freeze(d)                           Locks the dictionary permanently.
isFrozen(d)                         Returns true if locked, false otherwise.
val(d)                              Returns a deep-copied, frozen snapshot.
hash(x)                             Returns the native hash value of x (as int).
Copying & Mutability Matrix
There is no "unfreeze" function. Use copying to change lock states:
Syntax        Depth         Lock State          Best For...
b = a         Zero (Ref)    Same as source      Fast passing, default high-perf state.
(Loop copy)   Shallow       Outer unfrozen      Flat cloning, simple unfrozen shell.
b = copy(a)   Deep          Same as source      Exact deep clone, preserving lock states.
b = val(a)    Deep          Fully frozen        Read-only snapshots, safe dict keys.
b = clone(a)  Deep          Fully unfrozen      Complete rebirth. Fully mutable nested data.
* Loop copy: b = dict(); for ([k, v] in a) b[k] = v
set: ═══ set (Unordered Deduplicated Collection) ═══
sets store unique elements only. Duplicate insertions are silently ignored.
Elements can be of any type. sets use REFERENCE SEMANTICS (like lists/dicts).
Construction
s = set()                       Empty set (or use @{})
s = @{1, 2, 3}                  set literal syntax (recommended)
s = @{1, 1, 2, 2, 3}            → @{1, 2, 3} (duplicates auto-removed)
s = @{x^2 for (x in range(5))}  Set comprehension
s = toSet([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])     From array/list/string (deduplicates)
s = toSet("hello")             → @{"h", "e", "l", "o"}
Membership & Iteration
3 in s                          true if present, false otherwise (O(1) lookup)
for (x in s) { print(x) }      Iterates in insertion order
len(s)                          Number of unique elements
Element Operations (Unified Container API - mutates via reference)
add(s, val)                     Add element (no-op if already present)
remove(s, val)                  Remove element (error if absent)
discard(s, val)                 Remove element (silent if absent)
clear(s)                        Remove all elements
s.pop()                         Remove & return an arbitrary element
(Note: legacy functions setAdd, setRemove, setDiscard, setClear
are still supported).

a.setUnion(b)                   a ∪ b  — all elements in either set
a.setIntersect(b)               a ∩ b  — elements in both sets
a.setDiff(b)                    a \ b  — elements in a but not in b
a.setSymDiff(b)                 a △ b  — elements in exactly one set
a.setProduct(b)                 a × b  — Cartesian product (returns set of lists)
s.setPow()                      P(s)   — Powerset (set of all subsets, max 20 elems)
Operator Shortcuts (and Compound Assignments)
a | b                           Union (same as setUnion)
a & b                           Intersection (same as setIntersect)
a - b                           Difference (same as setDiff)
a ^^ b                          Symmetric Difference (same as setSymDiff)
a * b                           Cartesian product (same as setProduct)
a |= b                          In-place union (a = a | b)
a &= b                          In-place intersection (a = a & b)
a ^^= b                         In-place symmetric difference (a = a ^^ b)
Relation Predicates (return true or false)
a.isSubset(b)                   Is every element of a also in b?
a.isSuperset(b)                 Is every element of b also in a?
a.isDisjoint(b)                 Do a and b share no elements?
a == b                          set equality (same elements, any order)
Type Checks
isset(x)                        true if x is a set
type(s)                         → "set"
isempty(s)                      true if set has no elements
Conversion
toList(s)                       set → list (preserves insertion order)
toSet(list)                     list/array/string → set (deduplicates)
Reference Semantics
sets share the same underlying memory when assigned:
s2 = s1                      s2 and s1 are the SAME set
add(s2, 99)                  s1 now also contains 99
sets are tracked by the Garbage Collector (see: /help sys).
Immutability & Hashing (Native Value Hashing)
sets use the same Native Value Hashing engine as dicts.
`@{1.0, int(1), frac(1,1)}` will result in a set with exactly ONE element.
Elements MUST be hashable. Unfrozen containers will throw a TypeError
if inserted. Built-in functions that generate nested sets (like setPow
or setProduct) automatically freeze their inner containers.
Functions and namespaces are always hashable. Class instances are only hashable if frozen or if they define __hash__.
freeze(s)               Locks the set permanently.
isFrozen(s)             Returns true if locked, false otherwise.
val(s)                  Returns a deep-copied, frozen snapshot of the set.
hash(x)                 Returns the native hash value of x (as int).
Copying & Mutability Matrix
There is no "unfreeze" function. Use copying to change lock states:
Syntax        Depth         Lock State          Best For...
b = a         Zero (Ref)    Same as source      Fast passing, default high-perf state.
b = a | @{}   Shallow       Outer unfrozen      Flat cloning, simple unfrozen shell.
b = copy(a)   Deep          Same as source      Exact deep clone, preserving lock states.
b = val(a)    Deep          Fully frozen        Read-only snapshots, safe set elements.
b = clone(a)  Deep          Fully unfrozen      Complete rebirth. Fully mutable nested data.
Examples
chars = toSet("abracadabra")    → @{"a", "b", "c", "d", "r"}
3 in a                          → true
9 in a                          → false
@{1, 2}.isSubset(a)             → true
enum: Enums in JC2 are zero-overhead, compile-time generated frozen namespaces.
They provide a clean way to define a set of named constants.
• By default, the first item is assigned 0, and subsequent items auto-increment.
Inside an `enum` definition block, you can directly use language keywords
You can explicitly assign values to enum members. The values MUST be
compile-time constants (literals or simple constant-foldable expressions).
• If you mix types, auto-incrementing is only allowed after integer values.
Enums support scope modifiers just like classes and namespaces:
Anonymous enums can be used directly as expressions:
• Strict Same-Line Rule: For anonymous enums, the `{` MUST be on the same line as `enum`.
At compile time, an enum is evaluated and converted directly into a
frozen namespace. There is ZERO runtime overhead for building the enum.
Because it is a frozen namespace, it can be safely used as a dict key
or set element, and you can iterate over it:
for ([name, val] in State) { print(name, val) }
class: ═══ Classes, instances, Inheritance & Operator Overloading ═══
Defining a Class (Anonymous & Named)
class ClassName { ... }             // Named class (Syntax sugar)
const ClassName = class { ... }     // Anonymous class assigned to variable
• `class Name {}` is strictly syntactic sugar for `Name = class {}`.
• This allows seamless use of scope modifiers: `local class Temp {}`.
• Strict Same-Line Rule: For anonymous classes, the `{` (or `extends`) MUST be on the same line as `class`.
• 'init' executes automatically upon instance creation.
• Inside methods, `self` refers to the active instance.
• Methods support default parameters: `method(x, y = 0) = ...`
Static Members & Late Binding
Classes support static fields and methods using the `static` keyword.
Static members are evaluated at class definition time and belong to the class object.
class MathUtils {
static PI = 3.14159
static add(a, b) = a + b
MathUtils.PI                 → 3.14159
MathUtils.add(1, 2)          → 3
★ The Golden Rule of `self` (Late Binding):
In JC2, `self` is dynamically bound at runtime. It ALWAYS points to the receiver
(the object on the left side of the dot). Because static methods are just functions
stored on the class object, if an instance calls a static method via the prototype
chain, `self` will point to the INSTANCE, not the class!
class A { static test() = self }
A.test()                     → <class A>
Access Control & Constants (local / const)
JC2 reuses `local` and `const` to provide strict class encapsulation:
• `local`: Makes a field or method STRICTLY PRIVATE. It can only be accessed
via `self.name` inside the class's own methods. It is completely invisible
to external code and subclasses (enforced at the VM level).
• `const`: Makes a field read-only after initialization.
• Modifiers can be combined and applied to static members as well.
class Account {
const id = 12345                 // Public read-only
local balance = 0                // Private instance field
static local const MAX = 999     // Private static constant
local helper() = self.balance    // Private method
Self-Reference (The `class` keyword)
Inside any method, the `class` keyword acts as an expression that evaluates
to the current class object itself. This is useful for factory methods or
accessing class-level metadata.
clone() = class(self.x, self.y)
Field Access (Dot Operator) & Instantiation
p = Point(3, 4)              Calls init(3, 4)
p.x                          Read field
p.x = 10                     Write field (creates if absent)
★ Keywords as Property/Method Names:
After a dot `.`, any language keyword (like `match`, `class`, `in`, `if`)
is safely treated as a normal identifier. This allows you to call methods
like `regex.match()` or access properties like `obj.class` without syntax errors.
Furthermore, inside a `class` definition block, you can directly use keywords
as method or field names (e.g., `match() = ...`). This is safely allowed because
class bodies are strict declarative contexts.
instances use strict REFERENCE SEMANTICS (tracked by the Garbage Collector):
p2 = p1                    p2 and p1 share the exact same object
p2.x = 99                  p1.x is automatically 99
You can also force destructure instances just like dicts:
{x, y} = p                 Extracts p.x into 'x' and p.y into 'y'
Dynamic Reflection (String Indexing)
Instances natively support bracket indexing with STRINGS as a fallback for
field access. This allows dynamic reflection without needing special functions:
field_name = "x"
p[field_name] = 42         // Exactly equivalent to p.x = 42
★ Strict Type Safety:
If a class does NOT explicitly implement the `__getitem__` dunder method,
indexing is STRICTLY limited to strings. Attempting to use a number or
other type (e.g., `p[0]`) will throw a TypeError. Instances are not arrays!
Inheritance (extends / super)
class ChildClass extends ParentClass {
init(...) = { super.init(...); ... }
method() = ...         // Override parent method
• Single inheritance only. Child inherits all parent methods.
• `extends` supports expressions, allowing inheritance from modules (e.g., extends engine.GameEngine).
• `super.method()` dispatches to the parent class's implementation.
Operator Overloading (Dunder Methods)
Classes can inject logic into operators via double-underscore methods.
Dunder methods are inherited through the class hierarchy.
Arithmetic:
__lshift__ (<<)  __rshift__ (>>)
__bitand__ (&)  __bitor__ (|)  __bitxor__ (^^)
Reverse arithmetic (when left operand is NOT an instance):
__radd__  __rsub__  __rmul__  __rdiv__  __rmod__  __rpow__
__rlshift__  __rrshift__
__rbitand__  __rbitor__  __rbitxor__
Example: 2 * vec  calls  vec.__rmul__(2)
Unary:
__neg__()        Unary minus: -obj
Comparison:
★ Auto-Inference: You only need to define __eq__ and __lt__. The engine will
automatically infer !=, <=, >, and >= based on these two methods.
(Note: This assumes Total Ordering. If your class uses Partial Ordering,
you must define the other comparison dunders explicitly).
Membership:
__contains__(x)   Called by:  x in obj
(If not defined, 'in' checks fields, methods, and __getattr__ by default)
Indexing & Dynamic Attributes:
__getitem__(...dims)         Called by:  obj[i, j, ...]. Dims can be ints, strings, or slice objects.
__setitem__(...args)         Called by:  obj[i, j, ...] = val. The last argument is the value.
__getattr__(key)             Called when accessing a non-existent field: obj.key
__setattr__(key, val)        Called when assigning to any field: obj.key = val
Iteration & Callable:
__iter__()                   Returns an iterator object (usually `self`) for `for-in` loops.
(If not defined, 'for-in' iterates over instance fields like a Dict)
__next__()                   Returns the next value in iteration, or `none` to stop.
__call__(...)                Allows the instance to be called like a function: obj(args)
Conversion, Hashing, Matching & Lifecycle hooks:
__str__()    → str(obj), print(obj), f"{obj}", format("{}", obj)
__repr__()   → Custom representation in the REPL and object dumps
__len__()    → len(obj)
__abs__()    → abs(obj)
__bool__()   → bool(obj)
__hash__()   → Returns a hashable value (number/string). Allows the instance
to be used as a dict key or set element. (Must be paired with __eq__)
__match__()  → Returns a 'view' object (like a list or dict) to be used instead of
the instance during pattern matching and destructuring.
__del__()    → Finalizer called by the GC when the instance becomes unreachable.
(Note: Timing is unpredictable. Exceptions inside are silently ignored).
Method Resolution & Instance Overrides
When calling methods explicitly (e.g., `p.foo()`), JC2 checks the instance's
own fields FIRST, then falls back to the class. This allows you to override
a method for a single instance:
p.dist = () => 0           // Overrides the class method for 'p' only
★ Magic Method Bypass (Dunders):
For implicit operations (like `a + b`, `hash(a)`, `str(a)`), JC2 strictly
bypasses instance fields and ONLY looks at the class definition. This
guarantees that all instances of a class share the exact same mathematical
and hashing behavior, keeping data structures safe.
p.__hash__ = () => 1       // Ignored by the built-in hash() function!
p.__hash__()               // Explicit call: returns 1
hash(p)                    // Implicit call: uses the class's __hash__
Chained Method Calls
Methods that return `self` enable fluent-style chaining:
class Builder {
init() = { self.parts = list() }
add(x) = { self.parts = push(self.parts, x); return self }
build() = join(self.parts, "-")
Builder().add("a").add("b").add("c").build()   → "a-b-c"
Destructuring with Methods
Methods can return arrays/lists for destructured assignment:
class Point { coords() = [self.x, self.y] }
[px, py] = Point(3, 4).coords()
Introspection
type(p)                  Class name → "Point"
isinstance(p)            true if p is any class instance
isinstance(p, Point)     true if p is (or inherits from) Point
hasField(p, "x")         true if field exists
getFields(p)             All field names as stringmatrix
getClass(p)              The class definition object
getParent(Dog)           Parent class or none
Type Predicates (see: /help type)
isclass(Point)           true if argument is a class definition
isinstance(p)            true if argument is any instance
isfunction(sin)          true if argument is a function/closure
match: The `match` expression provides powerful structural branching and destructuring.
It evaluates a subject and executes the first branch with a matching pattern.
• Pure identifiers (like `x` or `PI`) always BIND to a new local variable.
• To evaluate an expression and compare its result (Value Assertion), you MUST
enclose it in parentheses `()`. Static literals (1, "a", 2+3i) don't need parentheses.
Patterns are strictly evaluated from left to right. This allows dynamic
assertions to use variables that were just bound earlier in the SAME pattern!
[a, (2*a)] => "Matches if the second element is exactly twice the first!",
{"x": a, "y": (a^2)} => "Matches if y is the square of x!",
Matches lists, realmatrices, complexmatrices, and stringmatrices.
Uses `,` for rows and `;` for columns to strictly match dimensions.
[x, y]       // Matches 1x2 row vector or List of length 2
Extracts the remainder of a list, matrix, or dict.
The `...` pattern can be placed anywhere in a list or matrix row.
It will dynamically capture all elements between the fixed head and tail.
[a, b, ...mid, c; ...res] => "Matches at least 3 cols, captures middle."
(Note: Only ONE rest pattern is allowed per row. If default values are used,
the rest pattern MUST be at the very end of the row).
In matrices, `...` can capture either remaining COLUMNS in a row, or
remaining ROWS in the matrix, depending on its position:
• Before a semicolon `;`: Captures remaining COLUMNS for that specific row.
• At the very end before `]`: Captures all remaining ROWS as a sub-matrix.
// 'rest_col' is the rest of row 1 (row vector).
// 'rest_rows' is a matrix of all other rows.
[...row1; ...row2; ...res]      // 'row1' and 'row2' capture the first two rows.
Extracts values by key/field. Supports shorthand `{a}` for `{"a": a}`.
(Note: For instances, it only matches data fields. For namespaces, it matches everything including methods).
The `...rest` pattern always returns a standard dict containing the remaining fields.
{name, age} if (age >= 18) => name + " is an adult",
Use `if` guard clauses with type predicates for type checking.
Patterns can be infinitely nested to extract deep data.
• Variables bound in a pattern are strictly local to that branch's body.
• Patterns are evaluated top-to-bottom. The first match wins.
• If no pattern matches, the expression safely returns `none`.
Classes can define a `__match__()` dunder method to customize how their
instances are destructured. When an instance is matched, the VM calls
`__match__()` and matches against the returned 'view' object instead.
init(x, y) = { self.x = x; self.y = y }
If `__match__()` returns `self` (the exact same instance), the VM
safely intercepts it and falls back to default field matching.
This allows dynamic conditional views without infinite loops.
macro: Macros in JC2 allow you to write code that generates code. They run at
COMPILE TIME (during parsing), taking Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) nodes
as input and returning new AST nodes to replace the macro call.
• Macros are defined using the `macro` keyword.
• They can take zero, one, or multiple parameters (AST nodes).
• They are executed immediately upon definition by the compiler.
• They fully support recursive calls when used inside `quote` blocks.
Use the `@` prefix to call a macro.
If a macro expects N arguments, you can pass N-1 arguments in parentheses
and provide the final argument as a trailing `{ ... }` block.
• `quote { ... }` packages a block of code into an ASTNode Block.
Note: A Block creates a new lexical scope when executed!
• `quote expr` packages a single expression or statement WITHOUT a block.
Example: `quote local x = 1` returns an Assign node, not a Block.
• `$` (Unquote) is used inside a `quote` to inject an existing ASTNode.
If a macro returns a List of AST nodes, JC2 will automatically flatten
(splice) them into the current scope. This is crucial for injecting
multiple local variables without trapping them in a Block scope.
Macros can recursively call themselves inside `quote` blocks to traverse
and transform AST nodes. When passing an extracted node to a recursive
macro call inside a quote, simply use the unquote operator `$`:
// Recursively transform left and right, then change + to *

using the `import @` syntax. See `/help import` for details.
To avoid accidental variable capture (name collisions) in macros, use
`gensym("prefix")` to generate a globally unique AST Variable node.
Macros receive and return instances of the built-in `ASTNode` class.
You can inspect and modify these nodes using pattern matching or direct
// x is now 20, y is now 10
token: ═══ Syntax Macros & Lexical Token Manipulation ═══
While `macro` operates on parsed AST nodes, `syntax` macros operate directly
on raw lexical Tokens BEFORE parsing. This allows you to invent entirely new
syntax or manipulate code at the character level.
Defining a Syntax Macro
syntax my_syntax(stream) = {
// stream is a TokenStream object
// You must return a valid ASTNode (e.g., by calling stream.parse())
return stream.parse()
Calling a Syntax Macro
@my_syntax { 1 + 2 }
• Syntax macros MUST take exactly one parameter (the TokenStream).
• The tokens are captured from the `{ ... }` block following the macro call.
Parsing Tokens back to AST
To return executable code from a syntax macro, you must parse the modified
TokenStream back into an ASTNode using its built-in parse methods:
• stream.parse(): Parses all remaining tokens into ASTNode(s).
If the tokens form a single expression or statement, it returns a single ASTNode.
If multiple statements are parsed, it returns a List of ASTNodes (which
auto-splices into the current scope).
• stream.parseOne(): Parses exactly ONE expression or statement.
Stops parsing and updates the cursor immediately after the first valid ASTNode.
Perfect for extracting arguments or conditions mid-stream.
The TokenStream Class
When using `syntax` macros, you receive a `TokenStream` object.
This built-in class provides a safe and convenient API for token manipulation:
stream.tokens()            Returns the underlying List of Token objects
stream.match(type)         Returns true and consumes the next token if its type matches
stream.consume(type, msg)  Consumes the next token if it matches, else throws an error
stream.peek()              Returns the next Token without consuming it
stream.advance()           Consumes and returns the next Token
stream.previous()          Returns the most recently consumed Token
stream.isAtEnd()           Returns true if the stream has reached EOF
stream.insert(idx, token)  Inserts a Token at the specified index
stream.set(idx, token)     Replaces the Token at the specified index
stream.remove(idx)         Removes the Token at the specified index
stream.parse()             Parses all remaining tokens into ASTNode(s)
stream.parseOne()          Parses exactly one expression/statement into an ASTNode
The Token Class
Each Token in the stream has the following fields:
type         (str)  The token type (e.g., "IDENTIFIER", "NUMBER", "PLUS")
lexeme       (str)  The actual text of the token (e.g., "foo", "42", "+")
line         (int)  The line number where the token appears
position     (int)  The character position in the source file
★ CRITICAL: Modifying Tokens
When changing a token's meaning (e.g., changing a PLUS to a STAR),
you MUST modify BOTH its `type` and its `lexeme` synchronously
(e.g., `i.type = "STAR"; i.lexeme = "*"`).
JC2 enforces strict lexical validation during parsing: the engine will
re-scan the `lexeme` to ensure it perfectly matches the specified `type`.
If they mismatch (e.g., type is "IDENTIFIER" but lexeme is "1"),
the engine will throw a TypeError to prevent invalid AST construction.
Common Token Types:
"NUMBER", "STRING", "FSTRING", "RSTRING", "IMAGINARY", "IDENTIFIER"
"PLUS", "MINUS", "STAR", "SLASH", "CARET", "PERCENT", "ASSIGN", "EQUAL"
"LPAREN", "RPAREN", "LBRACKET", "RBRACKET", "LBRACE", "RBRACE"
"COMMA", "SEMICOLON", "COLON", "DOT", "NEWLINE", "EOF", "ERROR"
(And all language keywords in uppercase: "IF", "WHILE", "CLASS", etc.)

error: In JC2, errors generated by invalid math operations, type mismatches,
or explicit `throw` statements will terminate the current script sequence.
throw "message"             Throws an exact string error message
throw expr                  Throws any evaluated value
When an unhandled error or exception occurs, JC2's VM unwinds the
call stack and prints a highly detailed, ANSI-colorized Traceback.
This pinpoints the exact file, script line, and function where the
error originated, traversing seamlessly through class dunder methods
All thrown values are automatically wrapped in an `Exception` instance.
• message:    The error description or structured data (can be any type).
• traceback:  The call stack when the error occurred.
• suppressed: A list of secondary Exceptions thrown inside `defer` blocks
You can explicitly throw custom exceptions:
The `catch` variable (e.g., `e`) receives the thrown value.
`try`/`catch` is an expression. It natively returns the value of the
`try` block if successful, or the value of the `catch` block if an error occurred.
You can directly destructure the thrown error object in the catch clause.
If the pattern match fails, the error is automatically re-thrown!
You can trigger `throw e` inside a catch block to bubble unhandled errors up.
Control flow signals (`break`, `continue`, and `return`) pass through
It executes a zero-argument function `f` and captures the result safely into a list.
isError(status)       → true if error, false if success
assert(cond)                  Throws if cond is falsy
assert(cond, "msg")           Throws custom message if falsy

Path Resolution (Script-Centric)
JC2 resolves all relative file paths based on the location of the
CURRENTLY EXECUTING script, not the terminal's working directory.
If `C:/project/src/main.jc2` calls `io.readFile("data.txt")`, it will
look for `C:/project/src/data.txt`. This allows you to build standalone,
portable JC2 packages and modules that bundle their own data files.

from the directory where you launched the executable.

import: ═══ Import (Code Reuse & Native Modules) ═══
The `import` command loads code into the current environment.
It supports both JC2 script files (.jc2) and native C++ modules.
Syntax
import module               Loads module/library and binds it to a variable (Recommended)
import "path"               Loads and executes a .jc2 file, returning its namespace
import @module              Compile-time import (loads macros during parsing)
★ Namespace Binding & Scope Modifiers:
`import lib` is syntax sugar for `lib = import "lib"`.
You can apply scope modifiers directly to the import statement:
const import math       →  const math = import "math"
local import utils      →  local utils = import "utils"
Native Libraries (independent DLL / SO files)
Native libraries are written in C++ and compiled as independent dynamic libraries
(.dll on Windows, .so on Linux) located in the `lib/` directory.
They are strictly isolated and provide high-performance functionality.
import libName              Load a native library into a namespace
Currently available:
image       BMP image generation & plotting
prob        Probability distributions & hypothesis tests
json        JSON encode / decode / pretty-print
bytes       Bare-metal memory & binary file I/O
socket      Low-level TCP/IP operating system bindings
window      Real-time Native GUI window rendering
latex       Bi-directional LaTeX compiler & serializer
ffi         Zero-dependency Foreign Function Interface (Windows x64 only)
tensor      N-Dimensional Tensor engine with Autograd
Native libraries take priority over .jc2 files with the same name.
Importing the same library twice is a safe no-op (deduplicated).
Script Modules (.jc2 / .jcb files)
import discrete             Loads discrete.jc2 (or discrete.jcb) into `discrete`
Compile-Time Import (Macros)
To use macros defined in another file, you MUST import them at compile time
using the `@` prefix. This ensures the macros are available to the parser
before the rest of your script is compiled.
import @my_macros
@generate_code()
★ Zero Runtime Pollution:
Variables and helper functions loaded via `import @` are strictly confined
to the compile-time environment. Once parsing is complete, they are
automatically cleaned up and will NOT pollute your runtime global scope.
Smart Path Resolution (Script-Centric)
`import` resolves relative paths based on the directory of the
currently running script, NOT the terminal's working directory.
Search order for `import utils` inside C:/project/src/main.jc2:
1. <exe_dir>/lib/utils.dll (Global Native Library)
2. Local Native Library (`utils.dll` in script dir, data/, modules/, lib/, workspace, etc.)
3. Precompiled Bytecode (`utils.jcb` in script dir, data/, modules/, lib/, workspace, etc.)
4. Exact name (`utils` in script dir, data/, modules/, lib/, workspace, etc.)
5. Source Script (`utils.jc2` in script dir, data/, modules/, lib/, workspace, etc.)
Once a module starts executing, its own directory becomes the
path context for any further imports or file operations within it.
Features & Safeguards
• Deduplication: Importing the same file/library twice is a no-op.
• Chained imports: A module can safely `import` other modules.
• Error propagation: Errors inside an imported file abort the import.
• Encapsulation: All definitions are strictly isolated inside the returned namespace.
• Private Variables: Inside a .jc2 module, variables declared with `local`
are strictly private and will NOT be exported to the final namespace.

addE.desc: Element-wise addition. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix. Also supports string concatenation.

subE.desc: Element-wise subtraction. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix.

mulE.desc: Element-wise multiplication. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix.

divE.desc: Element-wise division. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix.

idivE.desc: Element-wise integer division (truncating towards zero). Supports broadcasting.

powE.desc: Element-wise power. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix.

modE.desc: Element-wise modulo. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix.

eqE.desc: Element-wise equality comparison. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix. Also supports strings.

neqE.desc: Element-wise inequality comparison. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix. Also supports strings.

ltE.desc: Element-wise less-than comparison. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix. Also supports strings.

leE.desc: Element-wise less-than-or-equal comparison. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix. Also supports strings.

gtE.desc: Element-wise greater-than comparison. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix. Also supports strings.

geE.desc: Element-wise greater-than-or-equal comparison. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix. Also supports strings.

maxE.desc: Element-wise maximum. Supports scalar-scalar, scalar-matrix broadcasting, and matrix-matrix. Also supports strings.

Acof.desc: Returns the algebraic cofactor of the element at row r and column c.

blkdiag.desc: Returns the block diagonal concatenation of matrices A and B.

residual.desc: Returns the residual vector r = b - A*x.

seq.desc: Generates a column vector sequence from start to end.

color.desc: Enables ("on") or disables ("off") REPL syntax highlighting.

removeKey.desc: Removes a key from a Dictionary. Throws an error if absent.

any.desc: Returns true if any element in v satisfies function f.

init.desc: Constructor method. Called automatically when a new class instance is created.
examples: init(x, y) = { self.x = x; self.y = y }

__add__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the addition operator (+).

__sub__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the subtraction operator (-).

__mul__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the multiplication operator (*).

__div__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the division operator (/).

__mod__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the modulo operator (%).

__pow__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the power operator (^).

__radd__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads reverse addition (other + self) when 'other' is not an instance.

__rmul__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads reverse multiplication (other * self) when 'other' is not an instance.

__neg__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the unary minus operator (-self).

__eq__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the equality operator (==).

__lt__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the less-than operator (<).

__contains__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the 'in' operator (val in self).

__getitem__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads index/key access (self[i, j, ...]). Arguments can be integers, strings, or slice objects.

__setitem__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads index/key assignment (self[i, j, ...] = val). The last argument in the variadic list is the value to assign.

__str__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads string conversion (str(self), print, f-strings).

__len__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the len() function.

__abs__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads the abs() function.

__bool__.desc: Dunder method: Overloads truthiness evaluation (if, while, bool()).

__hash__.desc: Dunder method: Provides a hash value for dict keys and set elements. Must return a hashable type.

__iter__.desc: Dunder method: Returns an iterator object for for-in loops. Usually returns self.

__next__.desc: Dunder method: Returns the next value in an iteration, or none to stop.
examples: __next__() = { if (self.idx >= len(self.data)) return none; return self.data[self.idx++] }

__getattr__.desc: Dunder method: Intercepts access to non-existent properties (obj.key).

__setattr__.desc: Dunder method: Intercepts all property assignments (obj.key = val).

__call__.desc: Dunder method: Allows an instance to be called like a function.

__match__.desc: Dunder method: Returns a view object (e.g., list or dict) to be used for pattern matching and destructuring. Returning self falls back to default field matching.

__del__.desc: Dunder method: Finalizer called by the Garbage Collector when the instance becomes unreachable. Guaranteed to be called exactly once per object lifecycle. Note: Because JC2 uses a Mark-and-Sweep GC, __del__ is NOT called immediately when an object goes out of scope; its execution timing is unpredictable. Any exceptions thrown inside __del__ are silently ignored.

desc: Generates a globally unique AST Variable node.
Used in macros to create hygienic variables that will never collide with user variables.
Conditional branching statement.
Executes the body if the condition evaluates to a truthy value.
Supports chained `else if` and a final `else` fallback branch.
Braces {} are optional for single-statement bodies.
Returns the value of the last expression evaluated in the selected branch.
Note: The `(` MUST be on the same line as `if`.
See also: /help control
Fallback branch of an `if` statement.
Executes when all preceding `if` and `else if` conditions are falsy.
Can also be used as `else if (cond)` for chained conditions.
See also: /help if, /help control
Loop that repeats the body as long as the condition is truthy.
Braces {} are optional for single-statement bodies.
Use `break` to exit early, `continue` to skip to next iteration.
Note: The `(` MUST be on the same line as `while`.
See also: /help control

for.signature: for (init; cond; update) { body }  |  for (var in iterable) { body }
desc: C-style for loop or for-in iteration loop.
C-style: for (init; condition; update) { body }
Executes init once, then repeats body while condition is truthy,
running update after each iteration.
For-in: for (var in iterable) { body }
Iterates over arrays, vectors, strings, lists, dicts, sets.
Supports destructuring: for ([k, v] in dict) { ... }
Supports local scope: for (local x in arr) { ... }
Braces {} are optional for single-statement bodies.
Note: The `(` MUST be on the same line as `for`.
See also: /help control
examples: for ([k, v] in {a: 1, b: 2}) print(k, v)

desc: Object identity operator.
Returns true if 'a' and 'b' point to the exact same memory location (or have the exact same bitwise representation for value types).
Unlike '==', 'is' does NOT perform deep value comparison and does NOT trigger the '__eq__' dunder method.
It is an extremely fast O(1) operation.
Note: For Copy-On-Write (COW) types like matrices, 'is' exposes the underlying memory sharing state.
examples: a = [1, 2]; b = a; a is b  // → true

in.signature: for (var in iterable)  |  value in container
desc: Used in two contexts:
1. For-in loops: Iterates var over each element of an iterable.
Supported: arrays, vectors, strings, lists, dicts, sets.
2. Membership test (operator): Returns true if the value exists
in the container, false otherwise.
Supported: arrays, lists, strings, dicts (checks keys), sets,
and instances (checks __contains__, then fields, methods, and __getattr__).
See also: /help for, /help control
Immediately exits the innermost enclosing loop (for or while).
Cannot be used outside of a loop body.
See also: /help control
Skips the remainder of the current loop iteration and jumps
to the next iteration (or the condition check for while loops).
See also: /help control
examples: for (i = 0; i < 10; i += 1) { if (i % 2 == 0) continue; print(i) }

desc: Exits the current function and optionally returns a value.
If no expression is provided, returns `none`.
Note: `return` does NOT consume newlines. If you press Enter immediately
after `return`, it is treated as `return none`.
Can be used anywhere inside a function body, including nested blocks.
See also: /help control, /help scope
Pattern matching expression.
Evaluates the subject expression and matches it against a series of patterns.
Supports literal matching, variable binding, guard clauses, and deep destructuring
of lists, matrices, and dictionaries.
Use `,` to separate multiple patterns for a single branch.
Use `if (cond)` for guard clauses.
Use `_` as a wildcard or fallback pattern.
Returns the value of the executed branch, or `none` if no pattern matches.
See also: /help match (topic)
Pattern matching statement. Evaluates expr and compares against
each case value. Executes the first matching branch.
The switch body MUST be wrapped in {}.
Case branches do NOT require {} and absorb all statements until the next case.
Multiple values per case: `case val1, val2:`
No fall-through — only the matched branch executes.
Returns the value of the matched branch expression.
See also: /help control
A branch inside a `switch` statement.
Matches when the switch expression equals any of the listed values.
Multiple values can be comma-separated for a single branch.
Does NOT require {} and greedily absorbs statements until the next case/default/}.
See also: /help switch, /help control
The fallback branch inside a `switch` statement.
Executes when no `case` value matches the switch expression.
Does NOT require {} and greedily absorbs statements until the end of the switch.
See also: /help switch, /help control
Creates a namespace, or refers to the current namespace.
• `namespace Name { ... }` is syntactic sugar for `Name = namespace { ... }`.
• Can be used anonymously as an expression: `Math = namespace { ... }`.
• Inside the block, the `namespace` keyword evaluates to the namespace object itself.
• Variables declared with `local` are private and will not be exported.
★ Dynamic & Dict-Like:
Namespaces are fully dynamic. You can add, modify, or delete members
at runtime. They support all dict operations (keys, values, for-in).
★ True Singleton & Freezing:
Namespaces share state perfectly. Exported `const` variables remain
strictly immutable. You can lock the entire namespace with `freeze()`
to make it hashable.
Defines a new class, or refers to the current class.
• `class Name { ... }` is syntactic sugar for `Name = class { ... }`.
• Can be used anonymously as an expression: `Point = class { ... }`.
• Inside methods, the `class` keyword evaluates to the current class object.
• `init(...)` is the constructor, called on instantiation.
• `self` refers to the current instance inside methods.
• Supports single inheritance via `extends`.
See also: /help class (topic) for full details
examples: init(x, y) = { self.x = x; self.y = y }

desc: Declares that a class inherits from a parent class.
The child class inherits all methods from the parent.
Use `super.method()` to call the parent's implementation.
See also: /help class (topic)
Refers to the parent class's method implementation.
Typically used in constructors: `super.init(...)` to initialize
inherited fields, and in overridden methods to extend behavior.
See also: /help class (topic)
Refers to the current class instance inside a method body.
Used to read/write instance fields and call other methods.
Automatically available in all class methods — no declaration needed.
See also: /help class (topic)
Scope modifier: restricts a variable strictly to the current block.
Without `local`, variables automatically overflow to the function scope.
With `local`, the variable is forgotten when the enclosing `{}`, `if`,
or `for` block ends.
Usage forms:
local x = expr     Initialize block-scoped variable
local x += expr    Compound assignment to block-scoped variable
local x            Standalone declaration (captures outer 'x' by value)
★ Recommendation: While `local x = x` is legal, prefer `local x` for direct
capture, or use a new name (`local y = x + 1`) for better performance and clarity.
Works in destructuring (per-variable):
[local a, b] = [1, 2]       a is block-scoped, b is function-scoped
Works in loops:
for (local x in arr) { ... }
★ Closure Safety: If a lambda captures a local variable, its block
environment is safely preserved in memory.
See also: /help scope

ref.signature: ref variable = expr  |  ref variable  |  func(ref param)
desc: Scope modifier: binds a variable to an OUTER scope variable, or declares a pass-by-reference parameter.
Without `ref`, assignments inside functions create new auto-locals.
With `ref`, the assignment reads/writes the enclosing scope directly.
Usage forms:
ref x = expr       Assign to outer variable x (throws error on execution if x is absent)
ref x += expr      Compound assignment to outer variable (throws error on execution if x is absent)
ref x              Standalone declaration (silent on execution, throws error on subsequent use)
★ Recommendation: While `ref x = x` is legal, prefer `ref x` for direct
binding to improve performance and semantic clarity.
Works in destructuring (per-variable):
[ref a, b] = [1, 2]         a writes to outer, b is auto-local
{x: ref a, y: b} = obj      Same for dict destructuring
Pass-by-Reference Parameters:
addOne(ref x) = { x = x + 1 }
When calling `addOne(val)`, the outer variable `val` is modified directly.
If a literal, expression, or `const` variable is passed (e.g., `addOne(5)`),
it safely degrades to pass-by-value to protect immutability. Works seamlessly
with closures, UFCS, and class methods.
See also: /help scope, /help state
examples: swap(ref a, ref b) = { t=a; a=b; b=t }

desc: Scope modifier: gives a closure variable PRIVATE PERSISTENT memory.
Each call remembers the previous value of `state` variables,
but the outer scope variable (if any) remains completely untouched.
The initialization expression (e.g., state x = expr) is guaranteed
to evaluate and assign EXACTLY ONCE during the first execution.
Usage forms:
state x = expr     Evaluates expr EXACTLY ONCE. (e.g., state x = x captures outer x)
state x += expr    Captures outer x as initial state, then adds expr ON EVERY CALL
state x            Standalone declaration (captures outer 'x' at definition time).
If 'x' is undefined when the function is created, it will
throw an error IMMEDIATELY at definition time.
★ Recommendation: While `state x = x` is legal, prefer `state x` for direct
capture to improve performance and semantic clarity.
Works in destructuring (per-variable):
[state a, b] = [1, 2]    a has memory across calls, b resets each time
See also: /help scope, /help ref
examples: counter() = { state n = 0; n += 1; return n }

desc: Declares a strictly immutable constant. Any attempt to reassign or
delete the variable using the `delete` keyword will throw a runtime error.
Constants declared inside functions or namespaces are locally scoped.
Note: In the REPL, you can forcefully wipe a const using the `/delete` command.
See also: /help scope
examples: delete G           // ✗ Error: Cannot delete const

desc: Declares a static field or method inside a class.
Static members belong to the class object itself, not to its instances.
They can be accessed directly on the class without creating an instance.
See also: /help class
examples: class Math { static PI = 3.14; static add(a, b) = a + b }

desc: Removes a variable from the current scope entirely.
Works on ordinary variables and system constants (like PI, E).
Cannot be used to delete variables declared with `const`.
Built-in functions cannot be deleted. If a built-in is shadowed,
`delete` removes the shadowing variable, restoring the built-in.
See also: /help scope
examples: delete PI         // use resetConst() to restore

desc: Error handling construct. Executes the body; if any error occurs,
execution jumps to the catch block, matching the thrown value against `pattern`.
try/catch is an expression — returns the value of whichever branch runs.
Control flow signals (break, continue, return) pass through unaffected.
See also: /help error
The error handler block of a `try` statement.
The pattern receives the thrown value (can be of any type).
Supports full pattern matching and destructuring.
If the pattern match fails, the error is automatically re-thrown.
You can re-throw the error with `throw e` to propagate it upward.
Note: The `(` MUST be on the same line as `catch`.
See also: /help try, /help error
Throws a runtime error with the given value (can be of any type).
Unwinds the call stack until a `try/catch` block catches it.
If uncaught, prints a full stack trace and terminates execution.
See also: /help error
Loads and executes a .jc2 script module or native C++ library.
Using `import module` automatically binds the loaded namespace to a variable.
Using `import @module` performs a compile-time import, loading macros and
helper functions during the parsing phase without polluting the runtime scope.
Native libraries (image, prob, json, bytes, socket, window, latex)
take priority over .jc2 modules with the same name.
Importing the same library/module twice is a safe no-op (deduplicated).
See also: /help import (topic) for full details
Native boolean constant, acts as 1 in math.
It is a language keyword and cannot be overwritten or deleted.
See also: /help scope, /help control
Native boolean constant, acts as 0 in math.
It is a language keyword and cannot be overwritten or deleted.
See also: /help scope, /help control
Represents the absence of a value. Evaluates as falsy.
Functions without an explicit `return` return `none`.
It is a language keyword and cannot be overwritten or deleted.
See also: /help basic
Defines a compile-time macro.
Macros take an ASTNode as input and return an ASTNode.
They are executed during the parsing phase.
See also: /help macro (topic)
Defines a compile-time syntax macro (Token macro).
Syntax macros take a TokenStream object as input and must return an ASTNode.
They operate on raw lexical tokens before parsing, allowing custom syntax.
See also: /help token (topic)
Packages a block of code or an expression into an ASTNode without executing it.
Used inside macros to generate code.
Use the `$` prefix inside a quote block to inject (unquote) an existing ASTNode.
See also: /help macro (topic)
Schedules an expression to be executed when the current block scope exits.
Defers are executed in LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) order.
They are guaranteed to run even if the block exits early via return, break, continue, or throw.
Useful for resource cleanup (e.g., closing files, releasing locks).
